llm-frontier.name: LLM Frontier
llm-frontier.scope: How the 2017 Transformer became the modern LLM stack: decoder-only scaling (GPT-3), the LLaMA recipe and its parts (RMSNorm, SwiGLU, RoPE), efficient attention (FlashAttention, GQA), and a separate mixture-of-experts path from Sparse MoE through GShard, Switch Transformer and DeepSeekMoE to the DeepSeek models.

papers.title: Sparse MoE
papers.full_title: Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer
papers.sentence_en: Routes each token to a few expert feed-forward networks, growing parameters without growing per-token compute.
papers.research_why_en: Introduced a trainable gating layer that routes each position to a sparse top-k subset of expert feed-forward networks, with auxiliary load-balancing losses, so parameter count can grow without growing per-token compute. The DeepSeekMoE models on this roadmap (DeepSeek-V2 and DeepSeek-V3), and DeepSeek-V4 after them, are fine-grained descendants of this layer.

evidence.note: 5,962 citations, 560 influential (not re-fetched).

evidence.source: Cai et al., A Survey on Mixture of Experts in LLMs (arXiv 2407.06204)
evidence.note: Says sparsely-gated MoE 'has brought new vitality to this three-decade-old technology' and that Shazeer et al. 'pioneered a differentiable heuristic with auxiliary load balancing losses', the paradigm that became predominant.

evidence.source: Hugging Face blog, Mixture of Experts Explained (Dec 2023)
evidence.note: Its history section presents Shazeer et al. 2017 as the step that scaled MoE to 137B parameters through sparsity (not re-fetched).
Cites Shazeer et al. (2017) on the routing-collapse risk that its expert-level balance loss is designed to limit.

papers.title: Transformer
papers.full_title: Attention Is All You Need
papers.sentence_en: Replaced recurrence with self-attention plus feed-forward blocks; the architecture modern LLMs are built on.
papers.research_why_en: Replaced recurrence with multi-head self-attention plus position-wise feed-forward sublayers, wrapped in residual connections and layer normalization. Every later node on this roadmap modifies this block, scales it, or is a model built from it.

evidence.note: 197,457 citations, 20,997 influential (not re-fetched).

evidence.source: Sebastian Raschka, Understanding Large Language Models: A Transformative Reading List
evidence.note: Item 2, under 'Understanding the Main Architecture and Tasks'.
In Assignment 1, students implement Transformer components and a minimal training run.
Cites the Transformer as the step that 'replaced recurrence with attention' and presents Attention Residuals as the same idea applied over depth.

papers.title: RMSNorm
papers.full_title: Root Mean Square Layer Normalization
papers.sentence_en: Normalizes by the root mean square only, dropping mean-centering; used in LLaMA and most later LLMs.
papers.research_why_en: Dropped LayerNorm's mean-centering and bias and normalizes only by the root mean square, with comparable quality at lower cost. In the pre-norm position it became the normalization of LLaMA and nearly all later LLMs.

evidence.note: 2,114 citations, 119 influential (not re-fetched).

evidence.source: Zhao et al., A Survey of Large Language Models (arXiv 2303.18223), Section IV-B
evidence.note: 'it is suggested to choose the pre RMSNorm for layer normalization'.
'RMS Norm is universally adopted over Layer Norm in modern models.'
Pre-normalization with the RMSNorm function of Zhang and Sennrich (2019). The Kimi K3 report also cites RMSNorm (ref. 145) for its KDA output and LatentMoE.

papers.title: SwiGLU
papers.full_title: GLU Variants Improve Transformer
papers.sentence_en: Showed gated feed-forward layers like SwiGLU beat ReLU and GELU; now the default FFN in LLMs.
papers.research_why_en: Showed that gated feed-forward variants (SwiGLU, GeGLU) outperform ReLU and GELU feed-forward sublayers in the Transformer. SwiGLU became the default FFN of PaLM, LLaMA and most later LLMs.

evidence.note: 2,374 citations, 144 influential, for a 4-page arXiv-only note (not re-fetched).

evidence.source: Zhao et al., A Survey of Large Language Models
evidence.note: Recommends 'SwiGLU or GeGLU as the activation function'.
GLU variants 'are now standard in nearly all credible modern language models'.

evidence.source: Sebastian Raschka, The Big LLM Architecture Comparison
evidence.note: 'the more efficient SwiGLU has replaced activation functions like GELU.'
Replaces the ReLU non-linearity with SwiGLU, introduced by Shazeer (2020), following PaLM.

papers.title: GPT-3
papers.full_title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
papers.sentence_en: Scaled a decoder-only Transformer to 175B parameters and showed few-shot learning improves with scale.
papers.research_why_en: Scaled a pre-norm, decoder-only Transformer language model (the GPT-2 architecture) to 175B parameters and showed that few-shot in-context learning improves with scale. This set the decoder-only scaling paradigm that every later frontier LLM follows.

evidence.note: 64,864 citations, 5,569 influential (not re-fetched).
GPT-3 is one of the reference models used to discuss block design and activation choices.
Attributes its pre-normalization to GPT-3 ('Pre-normalization [GPT3]') and benchmarks LLaMA-13B against GPT-3 (175B).
'Following Kaplan et al. (2020) and the training setup of GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020), many of the recently trained large models have been trained for approximately 300 billion tokens.'

papers.title: GShard
papers.full_title: GShard: Scaling Giant Models with Conditional Computation and Automatic Sharding
papers.sentence_en: Scaled MoE Transformers to 600B parameters with top-2 routing, expert capacity and the balance loss most later MoEs reuse.
papers.research_why_en: Scaled MoE Transformers to 600B parameters with top-2 routing, expert capacity and the balance loss most later MoEs reuse.

evidence.note: v1 Tue, 30 Jun 2020 10:42:02 UTC, only version. Title: GShard: Scaling Giant Models with Conditional Computation and Automatic Sharding. Sec 2.2: 'The Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layer used in our model is based on [16] ...'. The aux loss in Alg. 1 line 13 is (1/E)·sum_e (c_e/S)·m_e, the fraction-routed times mean-gate form.
ICLR 2021 poster (the OpenReview page sits behind a bot-verification wall, so the ICLR virtual page is cited).

evidence.source: Cai et al., A Survey on Mixture of Experts in LLMs (arXiv 2407.06204)
evidence.note: Cai et al. survey. 'Simplifying the above design, GShard [25] defines a new differentiable auxiliary loss Laux using a differentiable approximation (the dot-product of mean gates and mean gating decisions per expert). ... Switch Transformers [34] and many other subsequent studies [26], [28], [33], [66] have embraced this Laux design'. Also: 'the methods proposed by GShard [25] remain the predominant choice in industry'. [25] = GShard, per the reference list.

evidence.source: Hugging Face blog, Mixture of Experts Explained (Dec 2023)
evidence.note: Post dated Dec 11, 2023: 'GShard replaces every other FFN layer with an MoE layer using top-2 gating in both the encoder and the decoder.' On expert capacity: 'This concept will become one of the most important concepts for MoEs.'
CS336 Spring 2025 Lecture 4. The routing slide lists 'Gshard (k=2), Grok (2), Mixtral (2)', and GShard is the first row of the routing-setup table.

DeepSeek-V3 Sec 2.1.2: 'Compared with traditional MoE architectures like GShard (Lepikhin et al., 2021), DeepSeekMoE uses finer-grained experts and isolates some experts as shared ones.' Mixtral (2401.04088): 'This formulation is similar to the GShard architecture'.

papers.title: Switch
papers.full_title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
papers.sentence_en: Routed each token to just one expert and kept the router in float32 for stability, scaling Transformers to 1.6T parameters.
papers.research_why_en: Routed each token to just one expert and kept the router in float32 for stability, scaling Transformers to 1.6T parameters.

evidence.note: v1 Mon, 11 Jan 2021 16:11:52 UTC (v2 30 Apr 2022, v3 16 Jun 2022). Comments field: 'JMLR'. In the paper: 'a simplified strategy where we route to only a single expert' and 'we cast the router input to float32 precision.'

evidence.source: Hugging Face blog, Mixture of Experts Explained (Dec 2023)
evidence.note: Dedicated section: 'Contrary to the initial idea of using at least two experts, Switch Transformers uses a simplified single-expert strategy.' The post also says Switch 'simplify the load balancing loss'; the Switch paper states its loss follows Shazeer et al. (2018) and GShard.

evidence.source: Cai et al., A Survey on Mixture of Experts in LLMs (arXiv 2407.06204)
evidence.note: Cai et al.: 'the Switch Transformer model [34] has shown that a top-1 gating strategy (as illustrated in Figure 4 (a)) can also yield competitive results, a finding that has been substantiated and adopted by later studies [63].' Also: 'Since the initial integration of MoE into transformer architectures [25], [34], [35]'.

CS336 L4 opens 'What's a MoE?' with a [Fedus et al 2022] figure. 'Per-expert balancing – same as the switch transformer'. 'Solution: Use Float 32 just for the expert router'. The routing table lists 'Llama 4 (maverick) 128 1 1', a 2025 model with one routed expert per token.
DeepSeek-V2 Sec 2.2: 'We use an expert-level balance loss (Fedus et al., 2021; Lepikhin et al., 2021) to mitigate the risk of routing collapse'.

papers.title: RoPE
papers.full_title: RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding
papers.sentence_en: Encodes position by rotating queries and keys so attention depends on relative offset; used by most LLMs.
papers.research_why_en: Encoded position by rotating queries and keys, so attention scores depend on relative offset. RoPE replaced absolute position embeddings in LLaMA and most later LLMs, and it is the base that context-extension methods and MLA's decoupled RoPE modify.

evidence.note: 6,864 citations, 561 influential (not re-fetched).

evidence.source: Zhao et al., A Survey of Large Language Models
evidence.note: 'RoPE or ALiBi is a better choice since it performs better on long sequences.'
'RoPE ... has become dominant for position dependence since 2024.'

evidence.source: LLaMA paper, Section 2.2; DeepSeek-V4 report, Section 2.3.3
evidence.note: LLaMA removes absolute positional embeddings and adds RoPE (Su et al., 2021). DeepSeek-V4 still applies partial RoPE, citing Su et al., 2024.

papers.title: FlashAttention
papers.full_title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
papers.sentence_en: Computes exact attention in tiles kept in fast on-chip memory, making long sequences far cheaper.
papers.research_why_en: Made exact attention IO-aware: tiling and recomputation reduce reads and writes between GPU HBM and on-chip SRAM, so attention memory grows linearly instead of quadratically with sequence length. It and its successors became the standard attention kernels in LLM training stacks and made long training contexts practical.

evidence.note: 5,618 citations, 478 influential (not re-fetched).
In Assignment 2 (Systems), students implement FlashAttention2 in Triton.
Item 6, under 'Scaling Laws and Improving Efficiency'.

evidence.source: Zhao et al., A Survey of Large Language Models
evidence.note: Presents FlashAttention as the attention optimization that, unlike approximate methods, keeps quality while cutting GPU speed and memory costs. Notes that it is integrated into training libraries such as Megatron-LM.
LLaMA's efficient causal attention 'uses the backward from Dao et al. (2022)'.

papers.title: LLaMA
papers.full_title: LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models
papers.sentence_en: Combined pre-RMSNorm, SwiGLU and RoPE in a decoder-only model shared with researchers; later open models follow its recipe.
papers.research_why_en: Combined pre-RMSNorm, SwiGLU and RoPE in a decoder-only model, trained it on more tokens than Chinchilla-optimal, and released the weights to researchers. This recipe became the dense baseline that later open models explicitly follow, including DeepSeek LLM and through it DeepSeek-V2.

evidence.note: 22,069 citations, 2,252 influential (not re-fetched).
'The micro design of DeepSeek LLM largely follows the design of LLaMA' (not re-fetched). DeepSeek-V2 then follows DeepSeek 67B for its normalization and FFN settings.

evidence.source: Sebastian Raschka, The Big LLM Architecture Comparison
evidence.note: Notes how 'structurally similar' 2025 flagship models still are, built on the same refinements (RoPE, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, GQA).
Describes LLaMA as a model line that shaped many later architectures.

papers.title: GQA
papers.full_title: GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints
papers.sentence_en: Shares each key/value head across a group of query heads, keeping quality while shrinking the KV cache.
papers.research_why_en: Generalized multi-query attention by sharing each key/value head across a group of query heads, giving near-MHA quality at near-MQA KV-cache cost. GQA became the default KV-sharing scheme in open dense LLMs (e.g., Llama 2 70B through Llama 4) and the efficiency baseline that MLA and DeepSeek-V4 measure against.

evidence.note: 1,920 citations, 145 influential (not re-fetched).
'Grouped Query Attention (GQA) offers a favorable trade-off between inference cost and performance.'

evidence.source: Zhao et al., A Survey of Large Language Models
evidence.note: Presents GQA as the trade-off between multi-query and multi-head attention and notes its adoption in LLaMA 2.

evidence.source: Sebastian Raschka, The Big LLM Architecture Comparison; DeepSeek-V4 report
evidence.note: 'Llama 4 uses Grouped-Query Attention similar to its predecessors.' DeepSeek-V4 uses BF16 GQA8 as its KV-cache baseline.

papers.title: DeepSeekMoE
papers.full_title: DeepSeekMoE: Towards Ultimate Expert Specialization in Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
papers.sentence_en: Split experts into many smaller ones and added always-on shared experts so routed experts specialize; the MoE in DeepSeek-V2/V3.
papers.research_why_en: Split experts into many smaller ones and added always-on shared experts so routed experts specialize; the MoE in DeepSeek-V2/V3.

evidence.note: v1 Thu, 11 Jan 2024 17:31:42 UTC, only version. Title: DeepSeekMoE: Towards Ultimate Expert Specialization in Mixture-of-Experts Language Models.
Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the ACL (Volume 1: Long Papers), August 2024, pp. 1280-1297.

DeepSeek-V2 Sec 2.2.1: 'For FFNs, we employ the DeepSeekMoE architecture (Dai et al., 2024).' DeepSeek-V3 Sec 2.1.2 (arXiv 2412.19437): 'For Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs), DeepSeek-V3 employs the DeepSeekMoE architecture (Dai et al., 2024).'

evidence.source: Cai et al., A Survey on Mixture of Experts in LLMs (arXiv 2407.06204)
evidence.note: Cai et al.: 'Differently, DeepSeekMoE [30], [67] introduces the concept of fine-grained expert segmentation ...' and 'Qwen1.5-MoE [102] and DBRX [28] adopt a similar fine-grained expert segmentation strategy.' On shared experts, the survey credits DeepSpeed-MoE [64] as the originator and lists DeepSeekMoE among the adopters, 'indicating its ascension to a mainstream configuration'. DeepSeekMoE itself says 'the prototype of shared expert isolation can be credited to Rajbhandari et al. (2022)'.

CS336 L4 closes with 'DeepSeek MoE v1-v2-v3 ... To wrap up, we'll walk through the DeepSeek MoE architecture.' Its [Dai et al 2024] slide reads: 'Smaller, larger number of experts + a few shared experts that are always on. (Used in DeepSeek / Qwen, originally from DeepSpeed MoE)'.

papers.title: DeepSeek-V2
papers.full_title: DeepSeek-V2: A Strong, Economical, and Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Language Model
papers.sentence_en: Introduced Multi-head Latent Attention, compressing the KV cache into a low-rank latent, in a large MoE model.
papers.research_why_en: Introduced Multi-head Latent Attention (low-rank joint KV compression with decoupled RoPE) and scaled fine-grained, shared-expert DeepSeekMoE to 236B parameters (21B active), cutting the KV cache by 93.3% relative to DeepSeek 67B. MLA was later adopted by DeepSeek-V3, Kimi K2/K3 and GLM-5.

evidence.note: 1,541 citations, 143 influential (not re-fetched).

evidence.source: Sebastian Raschka, The Big LLM Architecture Comparison
evidence.note: 'MLA is not new in DeepSeek V3, as its DeepSeek-V2 predecessor also used (and even introduced) it.'
'Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA), introduced in DeepSeek-V2' was 'subsequently adopted by Kimi K2 and Kimi K2.5', and K3 keeps it in its global-attention layers.

evidence.source: PyTorch blog, Using Muon Optimizer with DeepSpeed (Jun 3, 2026)
evidence.note: GLM-5 uses a 'Muon Split' technique that splits MLA up-projection matrices by head, which confirms MLA in GLM-5.

papers.title: DeepSeek-V3
papers.full_title: DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report
papers.sentence_en: Trained a 671B-parameter MoE cheaply, adding auxiliary-loss-free load balancing and multi-token prediction.
papers.research_why_en: Trained a 671B-parameter (37B active) MLA + DeepSeekMoE model on 14.8T tokens for 2.788M H800 GPU hours, and added auxiliary-loss-free load balancing and a multi-token prediction objective. Its recipe became the template for the 2025-2026 open frontier models (Kimi K2, GLM-4.5/GLM-5, DeepSeek-V4).

evidence.note: 4,271 citations, 443 influential (not re-fetched). The arXiv-linked duplicate shows 0.

evidence.source: Sebastian Raschka, The Big LLM Architecture Comparison
evidence.note: 'Kimi K2 is basically the same as DeepSeek V3, except that it uses more experts in the MoE modules.'

evidence.source: Forklog report embedding Andrej Karpathy's Dec 26, 2024 post
evidence.note: Karpathy: frontier-grade capability 'trained on a joke of a budget (2048 GPUs for 2 months, $6M)'.

V4 adopts DeepSeekMoE and the auxiliary-loss-free strategy, and keeps an MTP configuration 'identical to that of DeepSeek-V3'. Kimi K3 'adopts auxiliary-loss-free routing [27]', where ref. 27 is the DeepSeek-V3 report.

edges.why: GPT-3 uses 'the same model and architecture as GPT-2', a pre-norm decoder-only Transformer, scaled to 175B parameters.
edges.relation_zh: GPT-3 把 Transformer 大幅放大，看几个示例就能学会新任务。
edges.relation_en: GPT-3 scaled up the Transformer and found it could pick up new tasks from a few examples.
edges.relation_quote: We use the same model and architecture as GPT-2 [RWC+19], including the modified initialization, pre-normalization, and reversible tokenization described therein, with the exception that we use alternating dense and locally banded sparse attention patterns in the layers of the transformer

edges.why: LLaMA Section 2.2 normalizes each sublayer input with 'the RMSNorm normalizing function, introduced by Zhang and Sennrich (2019)'.
edges.relation_zh: LLaMA 用 RMSNorm 归一化每层的输入，让训练更稳定。
edges.relation_en: LLaMA used RMSNorm to normalize the input of every layer, keeping training stable.
edges.relation_quote: To improve the training stability, we normalize the input of each transformer sub-layer, instead of normalizing the output. We use the RMSNorm normalizing function, introduced by Zhang and Sennrich (2019).

edges.why: LLaMA Section 2.2 removes absolute positional embeddings and adds rotary positional embeddings (RoPE), introduced by Su et al. (2021).
edges.relation_zh: LLaMA 去掉绝对位置编码，改为在每一层使用 RoPE。
edges.relation_en: LLaMA dropped absolute position embeddings and applied RoPE at every layer instead.
edges.relation_quote: We remove the absolute positional embeddings, and instead, add rotary positional embeddings (RoPE), introduced by Su et al. (2021), at each layer of the network.

edges.why: DeepSeek-V3 'adopts Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) and DeepSeekMoE architectures, which were thoroughly validated in DeepSeek-V2'.
edges.relation_zh: DeepSeek-V3 沿用 DeepSeek-V2 的省内存注意力和混合专家。
edges.relation_en: DeepSeek-V3 reused DeepSeek-V2's memory-saving attention and mixture-of-experts design.
edges.relation_quote: To achieve efficient inference and cost-effective training, DeepSeek-V3 adopts Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) and DeepSeekMoE architectures, which were thoroughly validated in DeepSeek-V2.

edges.why: MLA is motivated as an alternative to MQA/GQA, which shrink the KV cache but whose 'performance does not match MHA'. MLA's cache is 'equal to GQA with only 2.25 groups'.
edges.relation_zh: DeepSeek-V2 像 GQA 一样压缩模型对前文的记忆，但质量不降。
edges.relation_en: Like GQA, DeepSeek-V2 shrank a model's memory of earlier text, but without losing quality.
edges.relation_quote: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) (Ainslie et al., 2023) and Multi-Query Attention (MQA) (Shazeer, 2019). However, these methods often compromise performance in their attempt to reduce the KV cache. In order to achieve the best of both worlds, we introduce MLA

edges.why: FlashAttention is an IO-aware exact algorithm for the Transformer's softmax self-attention, motivated by its quadratic time and memory cost on long sequences.
edges.relation_zh: FlashAttention 分块算 Transformer 注意力，快且精确。
edges.relation_en: FlashAttention computed Transformer attention in tiles, making it faster yet still exact.
edges.relation_quote: We propose FlashAttention, an IO-aware exact attention algorithm that uses tiling to reduce the number of memory reads/writes between GPU high bandwidth memory (HBM) and GPU on-chip SRAM.

edges.why: The paper tests GLU variants 'in the feedforward sublayers of the Transformer [Vaswani et al., 2017]', replacing its position-wise FFN.
edges.relation_zh: SwiGLU 用门控替换 Transformer 前馈层的 ReLU，效果更好。
edges.relation_en: SwiGLU swapped the ReLU in Transformer feed-forward layers for a gate, improving quality.
edges.relation_quote: We test these variants in the feed-forward sublayers of the Transformer (arXiv:1706.03762) sequence-to-sequence model, and find that some of them yield quality improvements over the typically-used ReLU or GELU activations.

edges.why: GShard: 'The Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layer used in our model is based on [16] with variations in the sparse gating function and the auxiliary loss being used.'
edges.relation_zh: GShard 把 Sparse MoE 专家层搬进 Transformer。
edges.relation_en: GShard moved Sparse MoE's expert layers from LSTM models into the Transformer.
edges.relation_quote: Scaling capacity of RNN-based machine translation and language models by adding Position-wise Sparsely Gated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers [16] allowed to achieve state-of-the-art results with sublinear computation cost. We therefore present our approach to extend Transformer architecture with MoE layers

edges.why: Switch Transformer: 'Lepikhin et al. (2020) adapts a Mixture-of-Expert model and addresses expert overflow by passing its representation to the next layer without processing through a residual connection which we also follow.'
edges.relation_zh: Switch 把 GShard 的 top-2 路由简化为每个词元只走一个专家。
edges.relation_en: Switch cut GShard's top-2 routing to one expert per token, making MoE simpler and cheaper.
edges.relation_quote: Contrary to these ideas, we instead use a simplified strategy where we route to only a single expert. We show this simplification preserves model quality, reduces routing computation and performs better.

In response, we propose the DeepSeekMoE architecture towards ultimate expert specialization.'

edges.relation_quote: For FFNs, we adopt the DeepSeekMoE architecture (Dai et al., 2024), a high-performance MoE architecture that enables training strong models at an economical cost.

borderline.reason: It is 12 weeks old (Jul 27, 2026). Its own report says it is 'built on Kimi Delta Attention [Kimi Linear] and Attention Residuals [a separate 2026 paper]', and Raschka calls it 'essentially a scaled-up production version' of Kimi Linear. By the standard used to exclude GLM-5, it mostly integrates components introduced elsewhere: KDA, AttnRes, NVIDIA's LatentMoE, MLA and Muon. Its distinctive result is real: it is the largest open-weight model and the first frontier-scale linear-attention hybrid (Lukyanenko review), with day-0 SGLang/vLLM support. That is not yet enough for a place on the map, which is at the 14-paper cap. It is the first candidate to add, together with Gated DeltaNet, if hybrid linear attention becomes the default.

ICLR 2025. It is the linear layer in the 3:1 hybrids of Qwen3-Next and Qwen3.5 (Raschka's hybrid-attention gallery). Kimi Linear's KDA 'builds on Gated DeltaNet' with finer gating, and Kimi K3 cites it (ref. 137) for its delta-rule recurrence. It opens the hybrid-linear mechanism line. Its citation count could not be retrieved.

borderline.short_title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models (Kaplan et al.)
borderline.reason: It opened LM power-law scaling (9,359 citations, not re-fetched), GPT-3 was sized in its regime, and both the Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4 reports still cite it. Chinchilla, a research core paper that is not on the roadmap, replaced its parameter-heavy allocation and is the result LLaMA builds on; neither scaling-law paper is on the map.

Opened KV-head sharing, and GQA explicitly generalizes it. DeepSeek-V4's CSA/HCA use 'shared key-value MQA', which revives it. GQA remains the variant most open dense models adopted. It is the first candidate if the MQA, GQA, MLA chain should be fully explicit (the map is at the 14-paper cap).

The most-cited attention alternative (9,678 citations, not re-fetched) and the root of the selective-SSM line. Mamba-2 layers run NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 hybrids, and Gated DeltaNet is framed as 'Improving Mamba2 with Delta Rule'. It would anchor an attention-alternatives branch above Gated DeltaNet.

Introduced KDA, a 48B/3B-active KDA + MLA hybrid that beats full MLA under an identical training recipe, with up to 75% less KV cache at 1M tokens. Kimi K3 scales it. It sits between Gated DeltaNet and Kimi K3 in the hybrid line.

NeurIPS 2025 Best Paper (Qwen team). A sigmoid output gate after attention removes attention sinks and stabilizes training. It ships in Qwen3-Next and Qwen3.5, and Kimi K3 cites it (ref. 98) for its gated MLA layers. It is a block-level refinement, too recent to judge against GQA/MLA-level changes.

The Cai et al. survey marks it as the 2024 trigger of open MoE growth. Architecturally it is a top-2 MoE on Mistral 7B with no new mechanism, and DeepSeek-V2/V3 defined the MoE design later models copied. On the mixture-of-experts path it is the runner-up and is not included: Semantic Scholar shows 2219 citations, and it prompted the HF post. Its paper says 'This formulation is similar to the GShard architecture', so it adds no mechanism and does not feed DeepSeek-V2. Adding it would exceed the 14-paper cap; it would hang off GShard as a leaf, but auxiliary-loss-free balancing would fit the chain better (see below).

The first 1T-parameter model trained with a Muon variant (MuonClip). Kimi K3 says it adopts Muon 'following Kimi K2'. llm-frontier.curation_notes: The map is at the 14-paper cap, so Chinchilla, AdamW, Muon and DeepSeek-V4 are left out and mixture-of-experts gets its own path. The mixture-of-experts papers meet the same evidence rule as the rest of the map. With GShard, Switch Transformer and DeepSeekMoE (all rated high), the map has 14 papers. The path is Sparse MoE → GShard → DeepSeekMoE → DeepSeek-V2 → DeepSeek-V3, with Switch Transformer as a one-step branch off GShard. Switch → DeepSeekMoE is not drawn: DeepSeekMoE builds on GShard and moves to more, finer experts, the opposite of Switch's top-1 routing. Mixtral is the runner-up: its routing follows GShard and it does not feed DeepSeek. Transformer → GShard is drawn because GShard replaces every other Transformer feed-forward layer with an MoE layer. GPT-3 → LLaMA and LLaMA → DeepSeek-V2 are not drawn because LLaMA (RMSNorm, RoPE) and DeepSeek-V2 (GQA, DeepSeekMoE) already have two incoming arrows.

retrieval.name: Retrieval & Recommendation
retrieval.scope: Two communities on one map. Recommendation runs from BPR through sequential (GRU4Rec, SASRec), graph (LightGCN) and generative (TIGER) recommenders. Text retrieval covers BERT re-ranking, dense retrieval and late interaction (monoBERT, DPR, ColBERT).

papers.title: BPR
papers.full_title: BPR: Bayesian Personalized Ranking from Implicit Feedback
papers.sentence_en: Learned to rank items a user interacted with above ones they did not; its pairwise loss is still a default.
papers.research_why_en: BPR treats implicit-feedback recommendation as ranking each observed item above sampled unobserved ones, and gives a generic SGD learner for any scoring model. Its pairwise loss became one of the most widely used training objectives in recommendation: FPMC, GRU4Rec, NGCF and LightGCN all train with it or a variant of it.

evidence.note: 6,990 citations and 1,491 influential citations (re-fetched), a very high influential share.
BPR is one of seven 'Fundamentals' milestones: 'It became one of the most widely adopted training objectives in recommendation research.'
'We employ the Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR) loss [32]'. NGCF (arXiv 1905.08108) says all compared methods optimize the BPR loss.
Uses BPR, applied over several sampled negatives, as one of its two pairwise ranking losses.

papers.title: GRU4Rec
papers.full_title: Session-based Recommendations with Recurrent Neural Networks
papers.sentence_en: The first to model a user's session with a recurrent network to predict the next item.
papers.research_why_en: GRU4Rec was the first work to apply recurrent networks to session-based recommendation, using session-parallel mini-batches and sampled pairwise ranking losses (BPR and its own TOP1). It opened the line of neural sequential recommendation.

evidence.note: 3,216 citations and 558 influential citations (re-fetched).

Sequential-models milestone: GRU4Rec 'was the first work to successfully apply recurrent neural networks to session-based recommendation ... This opened the floodgates for neural sequential recommendation, leading to SASRec'.

evidence.source: Pan et al., A Survey on Sequential Recommendation (2025)
evidence.note: Presents GRU4Rec as the representative RNN-based sequential recommender, the base of GRU4Rec+ and later RNN models.
'Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) were first applied to recommendation scenarios in GRU4Rec'.

papers.title: SASRec
papers.full_title: Self-Attentive Sequential Recommendation
papers.sentence_en: Replaced RNNs with causal self-attention over the interaction history; the most used sequential baseline.
papers.research_why_en: SASRec replaced Markov-chain and RNN models with causal self-attention over the interaction sequence for next-item prediction. A 2025 survey calls it the most popular sequential recommender, and it is the main reported baseline for both TIGER and HSTU.

evidence.note: 4,375 citations and 1,141 influential citations (re-fetched).

evidence.source: Pan et al., A Survey on Sequential Recommendation (2025)
evidence.note: 'SASRec [1] is currently the most popular SR model'.
SASRec is named in the sequential-models milestone with GRU4Rec.
Uses SASRec as the baseline ('identical configurations as SASRec'), and its appendix concludes 'SASRec remains one of the most competitive approaches in traditional sequential recommendation'.

evidence.source: University of Wroclaw RecSys seminar list (2026)
evidence.note: SASRec and LightGCN are the two model papers presented. This is a small student seminar, so it is weak evidence.

papers.title: monoBERT
papers.full_title: Passage Re-ranking with BERT
papers.sentence_en: Fine-tuned BERT to judge query-passage relevance for re-ranking; the reference cross-encoder.
papers.research_why_en: monoBERT fine-tuned BERT as a query-passage relevance classifier for re-ranking and became the top entry on the MS MARCO passage leaderboard, beating the previous best MRR@10 by 27% (relative). It was the earliest use of BERT for text ranking and the reference cross-encoder re-ranker.

evidence.source: Lin, Nogueira & Yates, Pretrained Transformers for Text Ranking
evidence.note: 'The earliest use of BERT for text ranking was reported in January 2019 [Nogueira and Cho, 2019]'. The book has a dedicated monoBERT section.
1,691 citations and 186 influential citations (re-fetched) for an arXiv-only paper.
Cites Nogueira & Cho 2019 as the BERT re-ranker, alongside DPR and ColBERT.

papers.title: LightGCN
papers.full_title: LightGCN: Simplifying and Powering Graph Convolution Network for Recommendation
papers.sentence_en: Showed graph recommenders need only linear propagation of ID embeddings over the user-item graph.
papers.research_why_en: LightGCN's ablations of NGCF showed that feature transforms and nonlinear activations do not help collaborative filtering. It reduces graph CF to linear propagation of ID embeddings over the user-item graph with a layer-weighted sum, and it became the standard graph CF model and baseline.

evidence.note: 5,852 citations and 958 influential citations (re-fetched).

evidence.source: Stanford CS224W, lecture 11 'GNNs for recommender systems'
evidence.note: The lecture readings are NGCF, LightGCN and PinSage (confirmed on the current course page).

evidence.source: University of Wroclaw RecSys seminar list (2026)
evidence.note: LightGCN is presented alongside SASRec (weak evidence).

papers.title: DPR
papers.full_title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
papers.sentence_en: A BERT dual encoder trained on question-passage pairs that beat BM25, making dense retrieval practical.
papers.research_why_en: DPR showed that a BERT dual encoder trained on question-passage pairs, with in-batch and BM25 hard negatives, beats BM25 by 9-19 points absolute in top-20 retrieval accuracy. That made single-vector dense retrieval with ANN search a practical first stage, and RAG used DPR as its retriever.

evidence.note: 7,366 citations and 1,098 influential citations (re-fetched).

evidence.source: Lin, Nogueira & Yates, Pretrained Transformers for Text Ranking
evidence.note: The dense-retrieval chapter is built around bi-encoders such as DPR and ANCE.
DPR is the worked example of representation-similarity retrieval.
'The retrieval component p_eta(z|x) is based on DPR'.

papers.title: ColBERT
papers.full_title: ColBERT: Efficient and Effective Passage Search via Contextualized Late Interaction over BERT
papers.sentence_en: Late interaction: encode query and document tokens separately, then score by summing the best token matches.
papers.research_why_en: ColBERT introduced late interaction: queries and documents are encoded separately into per-token BERT embeddings and scored by summing MaxSim matches. This kept quality competitive with BERT re-rankers while running two orders of magnitude faster, and it started the late-interaction line (ColBERTv2, PLAID, ColPali).

evidence.note: 2,664 citations and 284 influential citations (re-fetched).

evidence.source: Lin, Nogueira & Yates, Pretrained Transformers for Text Ranking
evidence.note: Has a dedicated section on per-token representations and late interaction (ColBERT).

evidence.source: LIR: First Workshop on Late Interaction and Multi-Vector Retrieval @ ECIR 2026
evidence.note: 'Late interaction retrieval methods, pioneered by ColBERT, have emerged as a powerful alternative to single-vector neural IR.'
vLLM serves ColBERT-style late-interaction models (ColQwen3, per-token embeddings scored with MaxSim). Seen in search results.

papers.title: TIGER
papers.full_title: Recommender Systems with Generative Retrieval
papers.sentence_en: Represents items as semantic ID codes and generates the next item's code: generative retrieval for recommendation.
papers.research_why_en: TIGER represents each item as a Semantic ID (RQ-VAE codes of its content embedding) and trains a seq2seq Transformer to generate the next item's code tuple, bringing generative retrieval to recommendation. It is the template that later semantic-ID generative recommenders follow.

evidence.source: Pan et al., A Survey on Sequential Recommendation (2025)
evidence.note: '[TIGER] is the first model that leverages semantic IDs for generative recommendation'.

evidence.source: Ju et al. (Snap), Generative Recommendation with Semantic IDs: A Practitioner's Handbook
evidence.note: 'TIGER (Rajput et al., 2023) first applied transformers to predict item SIDs for recommendation, extending ideas from GR in document retrieval (Tay et al., 2022)'. It also says RQ-VAE became the default SID tokenizer 'since its use by TIGER'.

evidence.source: NVIDIA Technical Blog, How Generative Recommenders Are Redefining RecSys at Scale (2026-08-20)
evidence.note: 'Architectures such as TIGER, PLUM, OneRec v1/v2' use Semantic IDs as their foundation.
483 citations and 98 influential citations (re-fetched), high for a 2023 recsys paper.

edges.why: LightGCN is trained with the BPR pairwise loss, citing Rendle et al. 2009.
edges.relation_zh: LightGCN 用 BPR 损失训练图嵌入：交互过的物品要排在未交互的前面。
edges.relation_en: LightGCN trained its embeddings with BPR's loss, ranking a user's items above the rest.
edges.relation_quote: We employ the Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR) loss [32], which is a pairwise loss that encourages the prediction of an observed entry to be higher than its unobserved counterparts

edges.why: GRU4Rec adapts BPR to several sampled negatives within a session as one of its two ranking losses, alongside its new TOP1 loss.
edges.relation_zh: GRU4Rec 借用 BPR 的成对排序损失来训练会话 RNN。
edges.relation_en: GRU4Rec borrowed BPR's pairwise ranking loss to train its RNN on user sessions.
edges.relation_quote: BPR: Bayesian Personalized Ranking (Rendle et al., 2009) is a matrix factorization method that uses pairwise ranking loss. ... We found the ones introduced in Section 3 (BPR and TOP1) to perform the best.

edges.why: SASRec calls GRU4Rec 'a seminal method that uses RNNs'. It keeps the goal of modeling long sequences, replaces recurrence with self-attention, and benchmarks against GRU4Rec and GRU4Rec+.
edges.relation_zh: SASRec 用自注意力取代 GRU4Rec 的逐步 RNN，一次看全部历史。
edges.relation_en: SASRec replaced GRU4Rec's step-by-step RNN with self-attention over all past items.
edges.relation_quote: the computation in each self-attention layer is fully parallelizable, which is amenable to GPU acceleration. In contrast, RNN-based methods (e.g. GRU4Rec [2]) have a dependency on time steps

edges.why: TIGER addresses the same next-item task as SASRec. It contrasts generating Semantic IDs with SASRec-style models that retrieve item embeddings by MIPS, and SASRec is its main baseline (up to 29% NDCG@5 gain).
edges.relation_zh: TIGER 像 SASRec 预测下一个物品，但生成语义 ID，不做向量检索。
edges.relation_en: TIGER kept SASRec's next-item task but generated semantic IDs instead of vector search.
edges.relation_quote: SASRec [17] ... perform an ANN in a Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) space to predict the next item. In contrast, our proposed technique, TIGER, uses Generative Retrieval to directly predict the Semantic ID of the next item.

edges.why: ColBERT's main BERT baseline is the Nogueira & Cho re-ranker. It keeps the BERT encoders but delays query-document interaction to a cheap MaxSim step, motivated by the 100-1000x cost of BERT rankers that it attributes to Hofstatter et al. and MacAvaney et al.
edges.relation_zh: ColBERT 分开编码查询和段落以提速，monoBERT 则逐对跑 BERT。
edges.relation_en: ColBERT encoded query and passage separately for speed; monoBERT ran BERT on every pair.
edges.relation_quote: (and the one adopted by Nogueira et al. on MS MARCO and TREC CAR) is to feed the query–document pair through BERT ... independently encodes the query and the document using BERT ... considerably speeding up query processing

borderline.reason: Direct parent of LightGCN, which ablates it, and a CS224W reading (S2: 4,127 citations, 653 influential). LightGCN showed that NGCF's GCN-inherited components are unnecessary and replaced it as the standard model. It would fit only if the roadmap were to show the simplification story.

The RecSys 2026 '20x20 milestones' guide names it the fundamentals paper of the latent-factor era (OpenAlex: 3,854 citations), and FPMC and GRU4Rec cite it. It is an alternative root for the recommendation line. The research preferred Koren et al. 2009 (Netflix MF) as the more cited (11,271) and more readable summary of the same model family; neither has an arXiv version, so neither is on the roadmap.

Confidence-weighted MF for implicit data (S2: 3,628 citations, 516 influential) and the basis of Spark ALS implicitPrefs. An IEEE Computer Society announcement (seen in search results) says it won the 2017 ICDM 10-Year Highest-Impact Paper Award, and FPMC cites it as one of the MF models it builds on. Its role overlaps with BPR and with Netflix MF, which is not on the roadmap because it has no arXiv version.

First web-scale GCN recommender, deployed at Pinterest (S2: 4,335 citations, 231 influential) and a CS224W reading. It is an industrial milestone, but the academic graph-CF line (NGCF -> LightGCN) only uses it as a baseline. It is the candidate that would link GraphSAGE, a collection member that is not on the roadmap, if the roadmap added a graph-industry paper.

Very highly cited (S2: 7,440 citations, 1,017 influential), and it triggered the academic wave of neural CF. However, Rendle et al. (RecSys 2020, arXiv 2005.09683) showed that a tuned dot product beats its learned MLP similarity, and it is absent from the RecSys 2026 milestone list, which picks YouTube DNN. Strongest candidate if the roadmap wants an academic neural-CF node.
Deployed in Google Play and very highly cited (4,341 S2 citations, not re-fetched). It opened deep CTR ranking, which is outside the stated scope; it should be core if a ranking/CTR line is added.

S2: 3,684 citations, 429 influential. It is a bidirectional, masked-item refinement of SASRec, and its reported gains were not consistently reproduced (Petrov & Macdonald RecSys 2022; Klenitskiy & Vasilev RecSys 2023). HSTU's appendix still finds SASRec 'one of the most competitive approaches'.

S2: 21,429 citations and 2,544 influential, about three times DPR. Its sentence-transformers library is the most common way to run embedding search, and CS224U lists SBERT with DPR as BERT-based representation-similarity models. It stays borderline because it targets sentence similarity and DPR does not build on it, but it is the strongest dense-retrieval candidate if the text-retrieval line widens to general embedding models.

Huge adoption and directly built on DPR ('The retrieval component ... is based on DPR'), but its contribution is retrieval-conditioned generation. It belongs on an LLM/NLP roadmap, with a cross-link from DPR.

ICLR 2025 (S2: 251 citations, 65 influential). It extends ColBERT's late interaction to page images with a vision-language model, and ColQwen models are now served by vLLM. It is the natural bridge from ColBERT to multimodal late-interaction retrieval, but too recent to call a line-opener; worth revisiting in 2027.

Concurrent with TIGER; it uses RQ-VAE Semantic IDs to replace random item IDs in a production YouTube ranker. It is strong adoption evidence for semantic IDs, but surveys and the Snap handbook cite TIGER as the origin of SID generative recommendation.

An end-to-end generative recommender from Kuaishou, building on the semantic-ID line; the only evidence cited is the later OneRec Technical Report (arXiv 2506.13695), which reports serving 25% of total QPS. That report had only 32 S2 citations. It is too recent to judge whether it opens a new line or refines TIGER/HSTU; worth revisiting in 2027.
The ANN infrastructure used by ColBERT, DPR and Facebook's embedding-based retrieval. It is an indexing system rather than a retrieval model, better cited in node text than shown as a node.
The standard logQ-corrected in-batch softmax for industrial two-tower retrieval. It is an important refinement of the YouTube DNN candidate generator, not a new line.

rejected_notable.reason: Neighborhood-CF prehistory before the 2009 latent-factor models. Item-based CF won the 2016 Seoul Test of Time Award, and the RecSys 2026 milestone guide lists GroupLens and Amazon item-to-item as application milestones. They have no direct inspiration edges into the roadmap papers.

The RecSys 2026 milestone guide lists it with GRU4Rec and SASRec under sequential models. It predates the 2009 latent-factor models, and FPMC is the Markov-chain model that SASRec explicitly generalizes.

Highly cited (S2: 3,148) and generalizes MF to arbitrary feature vectors, but it is the root of the CTR/feature-interaction line (FFM, DeepFM), which is outside the stated scope. It should be core if a CTR line is added.
The classical lexical baseline that every neural IR node compares against; prehistory for the text-retrieval line.
A single graph-convolution layer on the rating graph, superseded by NGCF and LightGCN, which explicitly contrast with it.
A CNN sequential recommender from the same period as SASRec, and outperformed by it; a refinement-level contribution.
An asynchronous hard-negative training refinement of DPR-style bi-encoders. Lin et al. present it alongside DPR as a training improvement, not a new paradigm.
Training-recipe and scale refinements of dense retrieval. They are widely used, but no single one opened a line.
Compression and serving refinements of ColBERT's late interaction, best noted in the ColBERT node text.
Learned sparse retrieval is a separate line not listed in this collection's scope. It would be reconsidered if a sparse-retrieval line is added.
Concurrent with CLIP and with the same dual-encoder recipe, but far less adopted in open tooling than CLIP, a research core paper that is not on the roadmap.
CTR-ranking refinements outside the stated scope; they would sit under Wide & Deep in a future ranking line.
No evidence yet of it becoming a default in deployed systems; the semantic-ID and HSTU lines have far stronger adoption evidence.
A generative entity-retrieval precursor that TIGER and DSI cite. TIGER and the GR survey credit DSI with structured semantic docids and call it the seminal GR work.

rejected_notable.short_title: Dacrema et al. 2019 / Rendle et al. 2020 (NCF vs MF revisited)
rejected_notable.reason: Important evaluation critiques that shaped recsys methodology, but they are not methods. Rendle et al. 2020 is cited in the NCF borderline note.
ANN graph-index infrastructure, like FAISS; not a retrieval or recommendation model.

collection_members_not_on_roadmap.reason: A general inductive GNN evaluated on citation, Reddit and PPI graphs. It is enormously cited (S2: 21,620 citations, re-fetched), but not as a recommender. Its recommendation impact arrives through PinSage, which NGCF describes as 'designed to employ GraphSAGE'. The graph-CF line that became standard (NGCF -> LightGCN) does not build on it directly. It belongs on a graph/representation roadmap, with a cross-link from the borderline PinSage.
A research core paper (CLIP) that is not on the roadmap; see the curation notes.

A gradient estimator for vector-quantized autoencoders (68 S2 citations, not re-fetched). In retrieval it appears only as an RQ-VAE tokenizer baseline in semantic-ID papers: QuaSID (arXiv 2603.00632) lists 'RQ-VAE-Rotation [6]', which 'replaces the STE in RQ-VAE with the rotation trick'. There is no evidence that it became standard in semantic-ID pipelines. It belongs on a representation or generative-models roadmap.

retrieval.curation_notes: Selection rule: high-confidence papers first, then papers that start or connect a line. The research kept 15 papers, 13 of them high. HSTU and DSI (medium) are left out. CLIP is left out as the only high paper with no arrow in the research; it remains on the collection list. Netflix MF, FPMC, DSSM and YouTube DNN are left out because every roadmap paper must have an arXiv version. FPMC → SASRec, Netflix MF → LightGCN and DSSM → ColBERT are therefore not drawn. DPR is shown without arrows: the research has no arrow between DPR and the other roadmap papers.

rl.name: Reinforcement Learning
rl.scope: Policy-gradient reinforcement learning and its path to RL for language models: the trust-region and advantage-estimation line that led to PPO, RLHF (Christiano, Ziegler, InstructGPT), and reasoning-oriented RL with GRPO and its successors.

papers.title: TRPO
papers.full_title: Trust Region Policy Optimization
papers.sentence_en: Updates neural policies by maximizing an importance-ratio objective inside a KL trust region.
papers.research_why_en: Extended Kakade and Langford's conservative policy iteration bound into a practical update for neural-network policies: it maximizes an importance-ratio surrogate objective under a KL trust-region constraint. PPO, and later GRPO, keep this surrogate but replace the hard KL constraint with ratio clipping.

evidence.note: 8,434 citations, 1,185 influential.

evidence.source: OpenAI Spinning Up, Key Papers in Deep RL
evidence.note: Listed under Policy Gradients together with A3C, GAE and PPO.

evidence.source: Berkeley CS285 Lecture 9, Advanced Policy Gradients (Fall 2020 slides)
evidence.note: The distribution-change bound is 'Proof based on: Schulman ... Trust Region Policy Optimization'; the lecture ends with natural policy gradient, TRPO and PPO as the practical algorithms.

evidence.source: A Survey of RL for Large Reasoning Models
evidence.note: 'PPO is proposed as a clipped surrogate objective of TRPO, which preserves the conservative policy iteration of TRPO'.

papers.title: GAE
papers.full_title: High-Dimensional Continuous Control Using Generalized Advantage Estimation
papers.sentence_en: A lambda-weighted advantage estimator that trades bias for variance; the default inside PPO.
papers.research_why_en: Introduced the exponentially weighted advantage estimator (lambda-weighted TD residuals), which trades bias against variance using a learned value function. It became the standard advantage estimator inside PPO, including PPO-based RLHF.

evidence.note: 5,064 citations, 634 influential; venue ICLR.

evidence.source: DeepSeekMath paper, section on PPO and GRPO
evidence.note: Describes PPO for LLMs as computing advantages 'by applying Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) (Schulman et al., 2015)' from a learned value function.
Calls GAE 'the state-of-the-art and canonical implementation in modern systems' for advantage estimation.

evidence.source: OpenAI Spinning Up key papers; Cameron Wolfe, GRPO overview
evidence.note: Wolfe: 'The critic can be used to compute the advantage via Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE)'. Spinning Up lists GAE among its key policy-gradient papers.

papers.title: Christiano RLHF
papers.full_title: Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences
papers.sentence_en: Learned a reward model from human comparisons of two behaviors and used it instead of a hand-written reward for RL.
papers.research_why_en: Showed that a reward model learned from human comparisons of trajectory segments can train deep RL agents on Atari and simulated robotics using feedback on a small fraction of interactions. This established the learn-a-reward-from-preferences recipe that RLHF for language models adopted.

evidence.note: 6,200 citations, 688 influential; venue NeurIPS (NIPS 30, 2017).
Assigned reading for the 'Reward Learning' lecture.
Presented as the application of RLHF to preferences between agent trajectories in Atari, the root of the language-model work.
Defines its method as 'reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF; Christiano et al., 2017; Stiennon et al., 2020)'.

papers.title: PPO
papers.full_title: Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms
papers.sentence_en: Replaced TRPO's constraint with a clipped objective; the default optimizer for RLHF and the template GRPO modifies.
papers.research_why_en: Replaced TRPO's constrained update with a clipped surrogate objective that allows several epochs of minibatch updates per batch. It became the default RL optimizer for RLHF (InstructGPT, ChatGPT) and the template that GRPO and its successors modify.

evidence.note: 32,340 citations, 5,333 influential, the highest in this field.
'Most early work on RL for LLMs used Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) as the default RL optimizer.'
Assigned reading for the Actor-Critic lecture.
PPO is the central algorithm. TRPO is described as 'accepted as the predecessor to PPO', and GRPO, GSPO and CISPO are presented as modifications of PPO's surrogate.

papers.title: Ziegler RLHF
papers.full_title: Fine-Tuning Language Models from Human Preferences
papers.sentence_en: First applied a preference reward model plus PPO to a pretrained language model, with a KL penalty to the initial model.
papers.research_why_en: The earliest work to fine-tune a pretrained language model with PPO against a reward model learned from human comparisons, with a KL penalty toward the original model (following Jaques et al.). The RLHF book says many canonical RLHF terms, such as reward models and KL distances, were formalized here.

evidence.note: Calls it 'the earliest work' in the language-model RLHF line, with 'many striking similarities to modern work on RLHF', and says canonical terms were formalized in it.
'Our methodology follows that of Ziegler et al. (2019) and Stiennon et al. (2020)'.
2,790 citations, 213 influential. Stiennon 2020 has more (3,575 / 350); see borderline.

evidence.source: Sebastian Raschka, The State of RL for LLM Reasoning
evidence.note: Lists it among the papers that predate InstructGPT: it 'illustrates the concept of PPO and reward learning to pretrained language models including KL regularization'.

papers.title: InstructGPT
papers.full_title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback
papers.sentence_en: Applied SFT, a reward model and PPO to GPT-3 for following instructions; the standard RLHF pipeline.
papers.research_why_en: Applied the SFT, reward model and PPO pipeline of Stiennon et al. (2020) to GPT-3 for general instruction following, with a KL penalty and a pretraining-gradient mix (PPO-ptx). OpenAI says ChatGPT was trained with the same methods, and it became the standard RLHF recipe that later LLM RL papers start from.

evidence.note: 25,112 citations, 2,509 influential; venue NeurIPS 2022.

evidence.source: RLHF book, Key Related Works (quoting the ChatGPT announcement)
evidence.note: Quotes OpenAI saying ChatGPT used 'the same methods as InstructGPT' with 'slight differences in the data collection setup'.

evidence.source: Sebastian Raschka, The State of RL for LLM Reasoning
evidence.note: Describes InstructGPT as the paper 'which described the recipe that was used to develop the first ChatGPT model'.
Both describe PPO as 'widely used in the RL stage of LLMs (Ouyang et al., 2022)' before introducing GRPO.

papers.title: GRPO
papers.full_title: DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models
papers.sentence_en: Dropped PPO's value network: each answer's advantage is its reward normalized within a group of answers.
papers.research_why_en: Introduced GRPO, a PPO variant without a value network. Each response's advantage is its reward normalized by the mean and standard deviation of rewards over a group of responses to the same prompt, and the KL penalty to a reference model moves from the reward into the loss. DeepSeek-R1, DAPO, Dr. GRPO and GSPO all start from it.

evidence.note: 10,151 citations, 2,974 influential. The influential share is very high for a 2024 paper.

evidence.source: TRL paper index and trainer list; verl README
evidence.note: GRPOTrainer is one of TRL's main trainers (GRPO and RLOO are the online RL trainers in its trainer list), and its loss options cover DAPO, Dr. GRPO, GSPO and CISPO. verl lists GRPO.

evidence.source: A Survey of RL for Large Reasoning Models
evidence.note: Uses GRPO as the base that 'DAPO, CISPO, Dr. GRPO, LitePPO' modify 'with careful tuning of sampling strategy, clipping threshold, and loss normalization'.
Points to DeepSeekMath as the source of GRPO but cautions that 'GRPO is not a special RL algorithm': it derives from PPO and has an advantage computation 'super similar' to RLOO's.

papers.title: DeepSeek-R1
papers.full_title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
papers.sentence_en: Showed large-scale GRPO with verifiable rewards on a base model yields long reasoning without SFT.
papers.research_why_en: Showed that large-scale GRPO with rule-based verifiable rewards, applied directly to a base model (R1-Zero), produces long chain-of-thought reasoning without supervised fine-tuning. Its released recipe and weights started the 2025 wave of open RLVR work, and the peer-reviewed version appeared in Nature.

evidence.source: A Survey of RL for Large Reasoning Models
evidence.note: Names OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek-R1 as the 'two recent milestones' showing that RLVR can produce long-form reasoning, and calls R1 'the first open-source model to match o1's performance'.
5,902 citations, 951 influential in about 21 months. Semantic Scholar indexes it under the Nature title.
'DeepSeek's results kick-started this revolution.'

papers.title: DAPO
papers.full_title: DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale
papers.sentence_en: An open, reproducible large-scale GRPO recipe with clip-higher, dynamic sampling and a token-level loss.
papers.research_why_en: Released an open, reproducible large-scale GRPO recipe built on verl, with four changes: clip-higher, dynamic sampling, token-level loss and overlong reward shaping. Its token-level loss normalization is now the default GRPO loss in TRL.

evidence.note: GRPOConfig defaults to loss_type='dapo' (token-level normalization), and epsilon_high=0.28 is recommended per DAPO.
Lists DAPO among supported algorithms.
2,981 citations, 609 influential; venue NeurIPS 2025 (also confirmed in the NeurIPS 2025 proceedings).

evidence.source: Cameron Wolfe, 'GRPO++: Tricks for Making RL Actually Work'; Interconnects
evidence.note: Wolfe opens his survey of GRPO improvements with DAPO's 'four key changes to the vanilla GRPO algorithm'. Lambert calls DAPO 'pretty much GRPO++'.

papers.title: Dr. GRPO
papers.full_title: Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective
papers.sentence_en: Showed GRPO's length and std normalizations bias training, and removed both for an unbiased objective.
papers.research_why_en: Showed that GRPO's per-response length normalization and standard-deviation normalization bias optimization, inflating the length of wrong answers. Removing both gives an unbiased objective whose advantage equals RLOO's up to a constant; the paper also showed that some R1-Zero behaviours, such as the 'aha moment', already exist in base models.

evidence.source: TRL GRPOTrainer docs and verl README
evidence.note: TRL offers loss_type='dr_grpo' and cites the paper for scale_rewards=False (question-level difficulty bias), although the default remains scale_rewards='group'. verl lists DrGRPO.
1,486 citations, 205 influential.
Listed as a Spotlight paper; the v2 PDF header reads 'Published as a conference paper at COLM 2025'.

evidence.source: RLHF book, Policy Gradients chapter; RL-for-LRMs survey
evidence.note: The RLHF book shows that Dr. GRPO's advantage equals RLOO's up to a constant factor. The LRM survey discusses it under 'The Struggle Between De-biasing and Normalization'. Lambert (Interconnects) notes it does not show better final downstream performance.

edges.relation_zh: PPO 保留 TRPO 小步稳妥更新的思路，改用简单的裁剪目标实现。
edges.relation_en: PPO kept TRPO's small, safe policy steps but used a simple clipped objective instead.
edges.relation_quote: introducing an algorithm that attains the data efficiency and reliable performance of TRPO, while using only first-order optimization. We propose a novel objective with clipped probability ratios

edges.why: PPO computes advantages with 'a truncated version of generalized advantage estimation'.
edges.relation_zh: PPO 用截断版的 GAE 来估计每个动作的优势。
edges.relation_en: PPO computed each action's advantage with a truncated version of GAE.
edges.relation_quote: Generalizing this choice, we can use a truncated version of generalized advantage estimation, which reduces to Equation (10) when λ = 1

edges.relation_zh: Ziegler RLHF 把 Christiano RLHF 用到语言模型上。
edges.relation_en: Ziegler et al. took Christiano et al.'s preference reward model from simulators to text.
edges.relation_quote: this work has only recently been applied to modern deep learning, and even then has only been applied to relatively simple simulated environments (Christiano et al., 2017; Ibarz et al., 2018; Bahdanau et al., 2018)

edges.why: InstructGPT states 'Our methodology follows that of Ziegler et al. (2019) and Stiennon et al. (2020)'.
edges.relation_zh: InstructGPT 把 Ziegler RLHF 的方法推广到通用指令。
edges.relation_en: InstructGPT reused Ziegler's reward model plus PPO recipe, now for general instructions.
edges.relation_quote: Our methodology follows that of Ziegler et al. (2019) and Stiennon et al. (2020), who applied it in the stylistic continuation and summarization domains.

edges.relation_zh: InstructGPT 用 PPO 微调 GPT-3，使奖励模型打分最高。

edges.relation_quote: Finally, we use this RM as a reward function and fine-tune our supervised learning baseline to maximize this reward using the PPO algorithm (Schulman et al., 2017).

edges.relation_zh: GRPO 沿用 PPO 的更新，但去掉价值网络，用一组回答的平均分作基线。
edges.relation_en: GRPO kept PPO's update but dropped the value network, scoring answers against their group.
edges.relation_quote: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a variant reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm of Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) (Schulman et al., 2017). GRPO foregoes the critic model, instead estimating the baseline from group scores

edges.relation_zh: DeepSeek-R1 用省资源的 GRPO 做大规模强化学习，训练推理能力。

edges.relation_en: DAPO openly reproduced and improved how DeepSeek-R1 used rewards to teach reasoning.

edges.relation_zh: Dr. GRPO 研究 R1-Zero 式训练，修正让错答变长的偏差。
edges.relation_en: Dr. GRPO studied R1-Zero-style RL and fixed a GRPO bias that made wrong answers longer.

borderline.short_title: Learning to Summarize from Human Feedback (Stiennon et al.)
borderline.reason: NeurIPS 2020, with 3,575 Semantic Scholar citations (350 influential) against Ziegler's 2,790 (213). InstructGPT follows it 'once again' for both the reward-model and PPO stages and names it with Christiano 2017 as the RLHF reference. Raschka credits it with 'the popular RLHF three-step procedure' that InstructGPT used, and the LRM survey cites it but not Ziegler. It stays borderline because it is a scaled-up refinement, by the same group, of the Ziegler 2019 recipe (reward model + PPO + KL). It would replace Ziegler if the roadmap preferred impact over origin.

borderline.short_title: RLOO / Back to Basics (Ahmadian et al.)
borderline.reason: ACL 2024. Revived REINFORCE-style optimization for RLHF with a leave-one-out baseline (from Kool et al. 2019). Adoption is real: RLOOTrainer is one of TRL's main trainers and verl supports it. The RLHF book presents RLOO as a main algorithm and shows that Dr. GRPO's advantage equals RLOO's up to a constant. It appeared three weeks after GRPO, which became the base of R1 and its successors, so including both would put two near-identical group baselines on the roadmap. Its citation count could not be retrieved.

borderline.short_title: Truncated Importance Sampling for rollout-training mismatch (Yao et al.)
borderline.reason: The primary sources are a Notion blog (Aug 2025) and an OPT 2025 workshop paper ('On the Rollout-Training Mismatch in Modern RL Systems'); the technique itself is Ionides (2008). The RLHF book calls TIS 'a crucial tool' for asynchronous LLM RL, the LRM survey cites it, and TRL turns importance-sampling correction on by default. But TRL's default mode is now sequence-level masking (MIS/IcePop-style), so the specific fix is already being superseded. It stays borderline until one off-policy correction settles.

Clips and stops the gradient through the importance weight instead of clipping the objective, so every token keeps a gradient. It has its own section in the RLHF book, is a TRL loss type, and was adopted by Meta's ScaleRL recipe (TRL documents epsilon_high=5.0 for it). The MiniMax-M1 report has 240 citations (27 influential), counting the whole model report. It is the strongest alternative to GSPO (not on the roadmap) as the 2025 ratio-control method.

Uses pass@k as the training reward to balance exploration and exploitation. It cites Limit of RLVR as motivation and is listed in the LRM survey. It has 138 citations (28 influential), more than PKPO's 93, but no library default, and arXiv 2511.16231 argues pass@k is a diagnostic rather than an objective.

Listed in Spinning Up's classic papers, and covered in CS285's advanced policy-gradient lecture (which cites Peters & Schaal 2008 for it). TRPO says its update 'is similar to natural policy gradient methods' and recovers NPG as a special case. Lilian Weng mentions it only in passing. TRPO is the node that made trust regions practical for deep networks, and no LLM RL method uses NPG directly.

TRPO's main theorem extends this paper's policy-improvement bound, and it is listed in Spinning Up's classic papers. TRPO already carries the idea. It would be the classical trust-region origin above TRPO, but it has no arXiv version.

Semantic Scholar shows 10,441 citations (1,343 influential), and it is on the Spinning Up and Lilian Weng lists. PPO compares against A2C and A2C with a trust region. Its asynchronous design was superseded, and the LLM lineage runs through PPO rather than A3C.

The classical truncated-importance-weight correction for decoupled actor-learner RL (covered by Lilian Weng). The LLM-era corrections do not build on it: the TIS paper cites Ionides 2008, and TRL cites Retrace (Munos et al. 2016).
Coined the name 'Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards'. The paradigm was popularized by DeepSeek-R1, and Tulu 3's RL stage uses PPO, so it adds no new algorithm.

borderline.short_title: ScaleRL (The Art of Scaling RL Compute for LLMs)
borderline.reason: A large compute-scaling study by Meta that proposes the ScaleRL recipe (CISPO loss among other choices); TRL documents how to reproduce it. It has 103 citations (13 influential) in a year and is an empirical recipe study rather than a new method.

rejected_notable.reason: Value-based deep RL, outside the policy-gradient scope. It is on syllabi (CS224R off-policy lecture) but is not an ancestor of LLM RL objectives.
Off-policy continuous-control actor-critic methods (Spinning Up key papers). No LLM RL method builds on them.
Offline preference optimization, not policy-gradient RL. It belongs on the post-training roadmap.
A turning point (the LRM survey pairs it with R1 as a milestone), but it has no technical paper describing the method (blog and system card only), so there is no citable algorithmic lineage.

A detailed report released alongside R1 that uses online policy mirror descent rather than GRPO. Lambert notes it lacked R1's open weights and viral moment, and the later GRPO-line papers build on R1, not on k1.5.
Incremental critic-free baselines. They are supported in verl and listed in the LRM survey's algorithm table, but they are not field-defining.
Incremental 2025 PPO/GRPO variants, each adjusting one component of the core nodes.
Listed by Spinning Up but superseded by PPO; no descendant in the LLM line.
Important for alignment data and AI feedback, but they apply the InstructGPT-style PPO recipe rather than changing the RL algorithm.
An early reasoning bootstrapping method that DeepSeek-R1 cites, but it is filtered self-training (expert iteration), not policy-gradient RL.

rejected_notable.short_title: Process reward models (Let's Verify Step by Step)
rejected_notable.reason: A reward-modeling contribution (process supervision), not a policy-optimization method. The R1 line uses rule-based outcome rewards instead.
Open reproductions of R1-Zero-style training. Lambert describes SimpleRL-Zoo as 'a more comprehensive version of OpenReasonerZero'. Useful replications, not new methods.

rejected_notable.short_title: Clip-Cov / KL-Cov (entropy mechanism of RL for reasoning LMs)
rejected_notable.reason: Entropy-collapse analysis with covariance-based clipping. verl supports it and the LRM survey lists it, but it is one of many entropy-control tweaks on GRPO/PPO.

collection_members_not_on_roadmap.reason: A research core paper (GSPO) that is not on the roadmap; see the curation notes.

A model technical report ('GLM-5: from Vibe Coding to Agentic Engineering', Feb 2026; Semantic Scholar shows 592 citations, 51 influential) describing asynchronous RL infrastructure and asynchronous agent RL algorithms. It applies this roadmap's methods at scale, and no evidence was found that others have adopted a specific algorithm from it. Better as a case-study reading than a node.

'Reinforcement Learning via Self-Distillation' (SDPO; ICML 2026, PMLR v306) has early traction: 332 citations, 73 influential. Its update distills the model's own feedback-conditioned predictions into the policy rather than using a policy-gradient estimator, which places it in the on-policy distillation line of the post-training collection (GKD is on its roadmap; OPSD is a research core paper that is not). It is also too new to judge.

The pass@k objective is in scope, and the LRM survey cites PKPO as the unbiased pass@k estimator. But PKPO (NeurIPS 2025) has 93 citations (16 influential), is not offered in TRL, and has no other evidence of adoption, and arXiv 2511.16231 argues pass@k is a diagnostic rather than an objective. It would hang off Limit of RLVR, a research core paper that is not on the roadmap, if the pass@k line matures.

Online RL for diffusion models through the forward process (ICLR 2026 Oral). This is diffusion-model RL rather than policy-gradient RL for language models, so it is outside this roadmap's scope; it is also a member of the Diffusion & Flow collection.

rl.curation_notes: Selection rule: high-confidence papers first, then papers that start or connect a line. The research kept 14 papers: 10 high, 4 medium. Fine-Tuning LMs from Human Preferences (medium) stays because it connects Christiano 2017 to InstructGPT. The other medium papers, Dr. GRPO, GSPO and Limit of RLVR, are all leaves. Of the three medium leaves, only the earliest, Dr. GRPO (March 2025), is shown to keep the map small; GSPO and Limit of RLVR are left out. GRPO → DAPO and GRPO → Dr. GRPO are not drawn, because DeepSeek-R1 already connects them. PPO → Ziegler and InstructGPT → GRPO are not drawn, because each would turn another kept arrow into a skip. PPO → InstructGPT and PPO → GRPO are kept, since GRPO is a PPO variant. REINFORCE and the Policy Gradient Theorem are left out because every roadmap paper must have an arXiv version (the panel shows its arXiv card). TRPO is the start (earliest paper, first row, no incoming arrow). TRPO → GAE is not drawn because it would turn TRPO → PPO into a skip.

diffusion.name: Diffusion & Flow
diffusion.scope: Continuous diffusion and flow models: the 2015 diffusion and 2019 score-based roots, DDPM and the score-SDE view, faster deterministic sampling (DDIM), guidance (ADM, classifier-free guidance), latent diffusion, the EDM design space, flow matching and rectified flow, and consistency models for few-step generation.

papers.title: Sohl-Dickstein
papers.full_title: Deep Unsupervised Learning using Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics
papers.sentence_en: Introduced diffusion models: slowly add noise to data, then learn to reverse the process step by step.
papers.research_why_en: Introduced diffusion probabilistic models: a fixed forward process that gradually destroys data with noise, and a learned reverse process trained with a variational bound. DDPM, Score SDE and the Flow Matching guide all trace the field back to it.

evidence.source: Flow Matching Guide and Code (Lipman et al., 2024)
evidence.note: 'Diffusion Models were originally introduced as discrete time Gaussian processes (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2020)'; verified in the PDF text.

evidence.source: Yang et al., Diffusion Models: A Comprehensive Survey of Methods and Applications (ACM CSUR)
evidence.note: Cites Sohl-Dickstein 2015 with Ho 2020 for DDPMs, the first of its 'three predominant formulations'; verified in the PDF text.

evidence.source: Lilian Weng, What are Diffusion Models?
evidence.note: Named first among the diffusion-based models the post builds on, with NCSN and DDPM; the Swiss-roll figure comes from this paper.

evidence.source: Yang Song blog, Generative Modeling by Estimating Gradients of the Data Distribution
evidence.note: 'Diffusion probabilistic models are hierachical latent variable models first proposed by Jascha and his colleagues in 2015'.

evidence.source: Semantic Scholar batch API (2026-10-20 query; not re-fetched)
evidence.note: 10,991 citations, 547 influential (not re-fetched).

papers.title: NCSN
papers.full_title: Generative Modeling by Estimating Gradients of the Data Distribution
papers.sentence_en: Trained one network to estimate the score (gradient of log density) at many noise levels and sampled with Langevin dynamics.
papers.research_why_en: Trained one noise-conditional network to estimate the score (the gradient of the log density) of data perturbed at many Gaussian noise levels, and sampled with annealed Langevin dynamics. This started the score-based line that DDPM connected to and that Score SDE later unified with diffusion models.

evidence.source: Yang et al., Diffusion Models: A Comprehensive Survey (ACM CSUR)
evidence.note: Score-based generative models (SGMs) are the second of the survey's 'three predominant formulations'.
Presents NCSN as the foundation of score-based generative modeling, with Score SDE as its continuous-time generalization.

evidence.source: Lilian Weng, What are Diffusion Models?
evidence.note: Has its own subsection, 'Connection with noise-conditioned score networks (NCSN)'.
Session 2 is 'Score-based generative modeling'.
6,122 citations, 513 influential.

papers.title: DDPM
papers.full_title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models
papers.sentence_en: Made diffusion work for high-quality images with a simple noise-prediction loss; its recipe became the standard.
papers.research_why_en: Showed that diffusion models generate high-quality images (FID 3.17 on CIFAR-10) when trained with a simple noise-prediction objective, and connected diffusion models to denoising score matching with Langevin dynamics. Its parameterization and objective became the standard recipe the rest of the field builds on.

evidence.note: 36,546 citations, 5,037 influential; the most-cited paper in this roadmap.

evidence.source: Yang et al., Diffusion Models: A Comprehensive Survey (ACM CSUR)
evidence.note: DDPMs are the first of the survey's 'three predominant formulations'.

evidence.source: OPIG blog, A timeline of sampling methods of diffusion models (2026)
evidence.note: Traces the field 'through four foundational works: DDPM, DDIM, the score-based SDE unification, and EDM'.

evidence.source: Lilian Weng, What are Diffusion Models?
evidence.note: DDPM is the central reference for the post's derivations and training objective.
'DDIMScheduler extends the denoising procedure introduced in denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs)'; eta=1 corresponds to DDPM.

papers.title: DDIM
papers.full_title: Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models
papers.sentence_en: A deterministic sampler that shares DDPM's training but needs far fewer steps, and maps noise to images invertibly.
papers.research_why_en: Built non-Markovian processes that share DDPM's training objective, giving a deterministic sampler that is 10-50x faster in wall-clock time and an invertible noise-to-image mapping. It became a default sampler and is the teacher that progressive distillation compresses.

evidence.note: 14,001 citations, 1,857 influential.
Core diffusers scheduler; 'A value of 0 corresponds to DDIM (deterministic)'.
The reference txt2img script exposes DDIM sampling (--ddim_steps, --ddim_eta); its default sampler is PLMS.

evidence.source: OPIG blog, A timeline of sampling methods of diffusion models
evidence.note: One of the 'four foundational works'.

evidence.source: Sander Dieleman, Learning the integral of a diffusion model (flow maps)
evidence.note: Cites DDIM (ref. 6) for the deterministic update rule that flow-map methods start from.

papers.title: Score SDE
papers.full_title: Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations
papers.sentence_en: Unified score models and DDPM as stochastic differential equations and introduced the probability flow ODE.
papers.research_why_en: Showed that score-based models (NCSN) and DDPM are discretizations of variance-exploding and variance-preserving SDEs. It introduced the probability flow ODE, predictor-corrector sampling and exact likelihoods. EDM, flow matching, rectified flow, consistency models and DMD all build on this continuous-time view.

evidence.source: Yang et al., Diffusion Models: A Comprehensive Survey (ACM CSUR)
evidence.note: Score SDEs are the third of the survey's 'three predominant formulations'.

evidence.source: Flow Matching Guide and Code (Lipman et al., 2024)
evidence.note: Diffusion models were 'later formulated in terms of continuous time Stochastic Differential Equations (SDEs) (Song et al., 2021)'.
'This work bridges both score-based generative modeling and diffusion probabilistic modeling into a unified framework.'
'The score-based SDE unification' is one of its four foundational works.
The course is built on the ODE/SDE view; lecture 3-A covers score functions, denoising score matching and SDE sampling.
12,622 citations, 2,045 influential.

papers.title: ADM
papers.full_title: Diffusion Models Beat GANs on Image Synthesis
papers.sentence_en: Showed diffusion models beating GANs on ImageNet, using a better UNet and classifier guidance.
papers.research_why_en: Showed diffusion models beating BigGAN-deep on ImageNet (FID 4.59 at 256x256, 3.94 with upsampling) through UNet architecture ablations and classifier guidance, which scales classifier gradients to trade diversity for fidelity at sampling time. Its UNet became the standard backbone of later pixel-space work; Flow Matching, for example, reuses it.

evidence.source: Paper Digest, Most Influential NeurIPS 2021 Papers (2026-03 edition; seen in search results, page behind a captcha)
evidence.note: Ranked No. 1 most influential NeurIPS 2021 paper. Semantic Scholar (not re-fetched): 13,400 citations, 1,204 influential.

evidence.source: Sander Dieleman, Guidance: a cheat code for diffusion models
evidence.note: Dhariwal & Nichol 'really drove this point home' that classifier guidance substantially improves sample quality.

papers.title: Latent Diffusion
papers.full_title: High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models
papers.sentence_en: Ran diffusion in an autoencoder's latent space, making high-resolution text-to-image affordable; the basis of Stable Diffusion.
papers.research_why_en: Ran diffusion in the latent space of a pretrained autoencoder and added cross-attention conditioning, which made high-resolution text-to-image training and inference affordable. It is the basis of Stable Diffusion and of most later latent image and video generators.

evidence.note: 'Stable Diffusion is a latent text-to-image diffusion model'.
